Reframed with the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) lens, the July 29, 2020 FOMC statement pairs policy backstops with a notably tighter bank credit channel:

- Credit supply and demand from SLOOS: Banks reported broad-based tightening of lending standards and terms for C&I loans to both large/middle‑market and small firms, as well as across commercial real estate categories. Household credit (credit cards, autos, other consumer loans) also saw tighter standards, higher spreads, and lower credit line sizes/approval rates. Loan demand weakened for C&I and CRE, with consumer loan demand mixed to softer. Banks cited a deteriorating or uncertain economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, and concerns about collateral values and industry-specific risks.

- Implications for the FOMC statement: While the statement notes improved financial conditions due to policy measures (zero rates, asset purchases, repo/ON RRP), SLOOS indicates that the bank lending channel remained restrictive. This constraint on the flow of credit—especially for SMEs and CRE—reinforces the Committee’s emphasis on “considerable risks” to the outlook and helps explain the commitment to maintain the 0–1/4 percent federal funds rate range and continued Treasury/MBS/CMBS purchases to support transmission.

- Net read: Policy actions stabilized markets, but pervasive tightening in bank credit standards and weaker loan demand point to persistent headwinds for growth and inflation. Relative to an FSR-only read, SLOOS tilts the assessment more negative.
